messages:
sam: RFC follow-up — we still need to pick an approach for private CP connectivity. Option A: ephemeral session proxies deployed into customer VPCs (short-lived outbound mTLS tunnels). Option B: static cross-account peering/VPC endpoints. Pros/cons below, looking for input.

jess: quick gut: ephemeral proxies reduce long-lived network exposure but add connection churn and operational complexity. :thinking:

andrew: agree. Also curious about route table scale — peering adds routes per customer, proxies push egress but keep route tables stable.

mina: can you list the biggest operational concerns for ephemeral proxies? cert rotation? metrics? failure modes?

sam: sure — main tradeoffs we saw in spike: 1) certificate lifecycle: ephemeral needs short-lived cert issuance flow (ACME-ish or our CA API), 2) connection density: per-customer many proxies -> more outbound connections to CP, 3) debugging: ephemeral -> harder to trace source IPs in logs unless we add transparent proxy headers, 4) cost: proxies use tiny infra in-customer; peering may incur cross-account data transfer.

jess: also: peering requires cross-account route maintenance and sometimes security review from customer's side. For regulated customers peering is often blocked.

andrew: if we go ephemeral, what does the network layout look like? e.g., subnets, NAT, SG rules.

sam: example sketch: deploy proxy in customer private subnet with egress via NAT GW to our CP region. Proxy establishes mTLS to CP and multiplexes tenant connections. Route table stays same, no peering. Pseudocode: 
```yaml
proxy: 
  replicas: 2
  runAs: daemonset
  egress: nat-gateway
  mTLS: true
  cert_ttl: 10m
```

mina: who owns the cert authority? we can't push private CA to customers. We'll issue ephemeral certs via our control plane and validate via ACME-style challenge?

jess: we discussed a short-lived cert signed by our CA, delivered over the bootstrap channel. Token exchange + attestation from customer's bootstrap agent. No CA distribution required.

andrew: still concerned about NAT capacity and per-customer TCP conn limits. If a customer has many concurrent sessions, NAT could be bottleneck. Any plan for connection pooling?

sam: proxy will multiplex and reuse CP connections, reducing NAT flows. We also have a fallback: if proxy detects high concurrency and peering is allowed, it can negotiate a temporary peering via infra API (requires customer's IAM approval) — sort of hybrid.

infra-bot: created ticket INFRA-3121 for ephemeral proxy automation and INFRA-3122 for peering temporary approval flow (https://git.company/redwood/infra/issues/3121).

mina: how do we handle observability? need tenant-level IP mapping in CP logs so we can tie requests to customer subnets when debugging. Otherwise traces show CP -> proxy IP only.

jess: propose adding an X-Forwarded-Redwood header with encoded source-subnet and proxy-id, and signing it to prevent spoofing. CP should log that header and our log parser can resolve it to customer.

andrew: security review: header propagation ok, but ensure we strip it on any downstream to avoid leaking. Also record audit entries for certificate issuance.

sam: agreed. Action items: 1) Sam + Mina to draft cert issuance flow doc (RFC-2026 depends on this) — due EOW. 2) Jess + Andrew to run a perf spike for NAT + multiplexing (test harness ticket INFRA-3123). 3) Spike for header signing and log plumbing (owner: Mina).

mina: noted. I'll add attestation diagram and sample token flow to the RFC PR.

jess: +1. If the customer explicitly wants peering, we'll default to static peering with route automation — but ephemeral will be the recommended default for self-serve.

andrew: fine by me. One more note: document expected failure scenarios in the RFC (proxy crash, NAT outage, stale certs).

sam: will add a failure modes appendix. Thanks everyone. :thumbsup:
